About: Orbits — The Four Conic Sections

Source

Lecture
L35 — Kepler orbits from first principles
Simulation
Top-down 2D orbit + cone-section diagram (Guided-Inquiry)
Concept
Eccentricity e picks the conic (circle / ellipse / parabola / hyperbola). Specific energy ε is derived from e at fixed angular momentum — sign(ε) tracks bound vs unbound. The right panel shows how each orbit is a plane cut through a cone.
Units
Natural units with GM = 1. Energies are specific (per unit mass), ε = E/m. Angular momentum held fixed via p = L²/GM.
Serves
Deriving the possible motions of planets and comets from first principles — the four conic sections.
Inquiry
Visit all four conics; find the parabolic edge where ε = 0; see that ε > 0 never closes.
Misconception
“A planet's path is just an ellipse” / “the shape is arbitrary.” In fact e fixes the conic and sign(ε) fixes bound vs unbound. (For Veff intuition, see L36.)

Guided Inquiry

1. Orient

The body is set on a circular orbit: e = 0, and the specific energy ε is negative. Press ▶ Play to start it moving, and locate the conic label on the canvas.

Press Next once the orbit is running.

2. Investigate

Slowly increase e using the slider below and watch what happens to the trajectory and to ε. What happens as the orbit gains energy?

3. Find the boundary

Push e up until the orbit first fails to close. Read the ε value on the derived readout at that edge. What is ε there?

4. Test the limit

Can you find any value of e that gives a bound (closed) orbit while ε > 0?

5. Resolve — visit all four

Use the preset buttons to jump through Circle → Ellipse → Parabola → Hyperbola.

Watch the conic label (canvas + Controls) and ε: it stays negative for the first two, hits exactly 0 on the parabola, and goes positive on the hyperbola.

Optional: probe e = 0.99 vs e = 1.01 to feel how sharp the parabolic edge is.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A small body goes round the Sun, pulled by gravity. One slider, the eccentricity e, picks the shape of its path from four families: a circle, an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola. Two readouts name the curve and give the body's specific energy ε.

What you'll learn

  • What the eccentricity e of an orbit tells you.
  • What the specific energy ε is, and how e fixes it.
  • How slicing a cone gives the same four curves.
The two panels and the controls. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • The Sun: the yellow dot. The faint grey rings are guides drawn round it.
  • The body: the teal dot, with a dashed line to the Sun and a trail behind it. The faint curve is the exact path.
  • The curve's name: the label at the top of the orbit panel. On the right, a cone with a cutting plane. Drag it to turn it.
See itChoose the Ellipse preset and run at 2× speed. Watch for: the body starting right of the Sun and tracing a loop with the Sun inside it but off centre, the label reading ellipse.

03

Every orbit here has the same angular momentum

The body always starts at its closest point to the Sun, moving counter-clockwise at right angles to the line to the Sun. Moving e changes where it starts and how fast, but never the angular momentum per unit mass, L = r v. Its value is set by the semi-latus rectum p = L²/GM, which is fixed at 1.5, so L = 1.225.

r(θ) = p / (1 + e cos θ)  ⟹  rp = p/(1 + e),  vp = √(GM/p) (1 + e)
θ is measured from the closest point. Then rp vp = √(GM p) for every e.

So raising e moves the start closer to the Sun and raises the launch speed. At e = 0 the speed 0.816 is exactly the circular-orbit speed at r = 1.5.

04

The energy depends only on e

Gravity is a conservative force, so the specific energy ε = ½v² − GM/r keeps one value all the way round. Put in the launch point and the e-dependence appears:

ε = ½vp² − GM/rp = GM (e² − 1) / (2p)
With GM = 1 and p = 1.5, ε = (e² − 1)/3.

So e alone fixes ε. Below e = 1 the energy is negative, at e = 1 it is zero, and above e = 1 it is positive. A negative ε does not mean negative kinetic energy. The potential energy −GM/r is negative and larger in size than ½v². The zero of potential energy is at infinity.

eεsign(ε)
0−0.333negative
0.60−0.213negative
1.000.000zero
1.50+0.417positive
2.20+1.280positive

The sim's ε readout is worked out from e. It is not measured along the path, and it does not change as the body moves.

See itChoose the Ellipse preset and run at 2× speed. Watch for: ε reading −0.213 and sign(ε) reading negative, both unchanged while the body goes round.
05

Negative energy gives a closed orbit, a circle or an ellipse

When ε is negative the body cannot go beyond r = GM/|ε|, because ½v² = ε + GM/r cannot be negative. It stays near the Sun, and the path is a circle (e = 0) or an ellipse (0 < e < 1) that repeats every lap. The Sun sits at one focus.

ε = −GM/(2a)  ⟹  a = p/(1 − e²),  T = 2π √(a³/GM)
a is the semi-major axis. The energy fixes a, whatever the shape.

The size grows quickly as e nears 1. For the same reason, a satellite needs an energy −ε per unit mass, its binding energy, to be taken from its orbit out to rest at infinity.

See itChoose the Ellipse preset and run at 4× speed. Watch for: the body fastest at the start, slowest at the far end after about 2.8 s, and back at its start after about 5.6 s, with the trail closing the loop.
06

Zero or positive energy leaves for good

When ε is zero or positive, ½v² = ε + GM/r is never zero at large r, so the body has a closest point but no farthest point. The path is open, and it never repeats.

At ε = 0 the path is a parabola (e = 1), and the body creeps away with its speed falling to zero at infinity. The launch speed is then exactly the escape speed at that point, √(2GM/rp). At ε > 0 the path is a hyperbola (e > 1) and the body is still moving at infinity.

v∞ = √(2ε),  cos θ∞ = −1/e
θ∞ is where the two arms of the path point. The body's path turns through 2 arcsin(1/e).

The edge is sharp only in the energy. At e = 0.99 the orbit is still an ellipse, but its lap takes 4112 time units, so in the sim it looks open.

See itChoose the Hyperbola preset and run at 4× speed. Watch for: ε reading +0.417, the body swinging round the Sun in a tight bend and leaving along a nearly straight line that does not come back.
07

The same four curves are the cuts of a cone

The cone panel shows why these four curves belong together. Slice a double cone with a plane. A plane square-on to the axis cuts a circle. Tilting it gives an ellipse. When the plane is parallel to the cone's slanting side the cut is a parabola. Tilted more, it cuts both halves of the cone and gives a hyperbola.

For a real cone with half-angle α, and a plane tilted by β from square-on, e = sin β / cos α. The parabola, e = 1, comes at β = 90° − α.

The sim's cone has α = 35.75°, so the parabola sits at a tilt of 54.25°. The sim tilts the plane in proportion to e up to e = 1, so the picture shows the right kind of curve but not the exact e. At e = 0.60 a real cone would give e = 0.66. The cone is geometry only. It does not say why gravity gives these curves.

See itChoose the Parabola preset. Watch for: the plane tilted to run parallel to one side of the cone, a blue cut, the label parabola in the legend, and "current: parabola · e = 1.00" under the cone.
08

Where it matters

  • Escape speed. A circular orbit at radius r has speed √(GM/r). Launching √2 times faster at that point gives the parabola, and anything faster gives a hyperbola. At Earth's surface that is 7.91 km/s for the circle and 11.19 km/s to escape.
  • Satellite energy. A satellite of mass m on a circular orbit has E = −GMm/(2r), so its binding energy is GMm/(2r). For 1000 kg at the space station's radius of 6771 km, that is about 29 GJ.
  • Comets. Halley's comet has e = 0.967 and comes back about every 76 years. A visitor such as ʻOumuamua, with e ≈ 1.2, comes from far away, passes once and does not return.
  • Gravity assist. A spacecraft flying past a planet follows a hyperbola around that planet. It enters and leaves at the same speed in that frame, but its direction changes by 2 arcsin(1/e).
  • Real limits. The sim is a point body in a fixed 1/r² field. It holds L fixed, so changing e also moves the start point. Real orbits are also disturbed by other bodies.
09

Summary

In one line. Under inverse-square gravity every orbit is one of four curves, the conic sections.

Key points

  • r(θ) = p/(1 + e cos θ), with the Sun at one focus.
  • ε = ½v² − GM/r = GM(e² − 1)/(2p), and the same value holds all round the orbit.
  • For a closed orbit ε = −GM/(2a). For an open one v∞ = √(2ε).
  • e = 0 circle, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.

Common mix-ups

  • "Negative energy means negative kinetic energy." Kinetic energy is never negative. ε is negative because the potential energy −GM/r outweighs it.
  • "The Sun is at the centre of the ellipse." It sits at one focus. The centre is a distance ae away.
  • "A parabola is just a very long ellipse." An ellipse repeats, however long. A parabola has ε = 0 and never returns.

Things to try on your own

  • Compare the presets e = 0.99 and e = 1.01 and watch ε and sign(ε).
  • Set e to 2.2 and see how a very hyperbolic path bends only a little.
  • Drag the cone to look at each cut from the side.
